answer:
Overall assessment: The concept is intuitive and values-aligned, but the business model is not yet viable as presented, and scalability is doubtful without fundamentally better unit economics. The plan is a concept with a prototype, not a validated model.

Path to revenue: Revenue streams are plausible (per-jar fee to makers, mailer fee to customers, premium dashboard) but nothing is priced or tested. The central claim, that a per-jar fee will be lower than buying new jars, is almost certainly shaky. New glass jars typically cost roughly $0.50-$2.00 wholesale. A returned jar must bear outbound postage (prepaid mailer, likely $4-8 for a heavy glass item), packaging, labor to de-wax, wash, sanitize and inspect, breakage losses, and then return shipping to the maker. Realistic fully loaded cost per cycle is plausibly several dollars, well above the cost of a new jar. The value proposition therefore cannot be cost savings; it must be a sustainability premium that makers can pass on to customers, and that willingness to pay is unproven. Dashboard premium features are a weak monetization lever for tiny makers with limited marketing budgets.

Validity of assumptions: (1) Customer behavior: the plan itself admits the main competitor is customers doing nothing. Return rates are the make-or-break variable and are unaddressed; no incentive design (deposit, discount on refill, loyalty credit) is described, and no return-rate data exists. Typical voluntary return programs see low single-digit to low double-digit participation. (2) Maker demand: feedback from friends, family and a few local makers saying the idea is 'interesting' is not evidence of willingness to pay. No letters of intent, paid pilots or pricing tests. (3) Logistics: jars are heavy and fragile, creating breakage, shipping cost and carbon trade-offs; the plan claims carbon savings without acknowledging that round-trip shipping can offset or exceed avoided glass production. Also, jar heterogeneity across many small makers (sizes, labels, adhesives, wax types) complicates standardized cleaning and could require manual sorting. (4) Cost curve: 'cost per jar will come down with scale' is asserted, but postage and handling are largely variable costs, so scale economies may be modest. (5) Market sizing: no TAM/SAM/SOM; 'thousands of makers' is a count, not a revenue opportunity. Most small makers sell low volumes, so jars per maker may be small, requiring many partners to reach meaningful throughput.

Scalability: Operations are labor-intensive and run from a shared kitchen; scaling to thousands of jars/month requires dedicated space, food-safe or at least consistent sanitation processes, and possibly regulatory/health and insurance considerations. Geographic dispersion implies high shipping costs; a regional hub model (local makers, drop-off points, local pickup, standardized jar types) would be more economical than national mail-back. Two-sided network dynamics (makers need customers returning jars; customers need participating makers) are not addressed. Defensibility is low: larger brands and general reuse platforms (e.g., packaging reuse services) could add candle jars, and the dashboard is easily replicated.

Strengths: Clear, relatable problem; focused niche; complementary student skill set (operations, product design, software); low-cost, iterative start; honest acknowledgment of unknowns and of customer inertia as the true competitor.

Gaps: No pricing, financial model, unit economics, break-even math, return-rate assumptions, legal entity, website, advisors or evidence of paid demand. Funding ask is reasonable in scale but the use of funds (more mailers and equipment) scales an unvalidated model before testing key assumptions.

Recommendations: (1) Build a per-jar unit economics model with real postage, labor, breakage and supply costs. (2) Run a paid pilot with 3-5 makers testing price points and return-incentive designs (deposit-return, refill discount) and measure actual return rates. (3) Consider a local/regional hub or drop-off model to cut shipping cost and emissions. (4) Standardize jar types with partner makers to simplify processing. (5) Validate carbon claims with a lifecycle comparison including transport. (6) Secure two or three signed pilot commitments and a logistics or consumer-products advisor.

Bottom line: Promising mission and sensible niche, but viability hinges on unproven return rates and likely unfavorable per-jar economics; scalability is limited unless the model shifts toward regional density and a sustainability-premium value proposition validated with paying partners.
